summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies: EO 14168 on binary sex classification in documents, federal facilities and care funding; EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding; and EO 14201 on athletic participation, the last paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all United States identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth; new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents; and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker, available from 2022, has been eliminated for new applications. The policy is challenged in federal courts, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs; trans and nonbinary travelers have reported passports confiscated or blocked, leaving some stranded abroad.

Same-sex marriage sits in an unresolved posture. The 2015 federal marriage ruling's applicability was publicly contested by territory officials: in 2015 the territory's Attorney General said applicability was still under review while other US territories moved to apply it, and in January 2016 a newly confirmed District Court judge told the Senate he had not read the decision and would not perform same-sex weddings absent changed local law. A 2026 law review article by attorneys practicing in American Samoa concludes the ruling does apply and that the territory would have to issue a certificate to any same-sex couple that applied, while noting no couple has yet applied; the litigation path runs through the High Court of American Samoa (defendant the Territorial Registrar) and then the US Department of the Interior. Meanwhile a local ban is treated on-island as operative: the Fono Senate rejected a bill to outlaw same-sex marriage in March 2003, but a July 2024 survey by a Miami University law professor was still testing whether the existing ban would survive a 14th Amendment challenge.

Trans-specific violence and employment discrimination have been documented. In September 2023 the US Justice Department settled an employment-discrimination case with the American Samoa Government over harassment of a transgender employee; a June 2023 federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's suit against the territorial government over her gender identity; and in February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Local culture frames fa'afafine as a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture. The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS), formed in 2010, anchors this identity in cultural pride, and the Samoan islands are described as the homeland of fa'afafine culture. A 2009 travel column reported that homosexuality is widely accepted in Samoan culture, though reserved behavior is expected of people of all orientations under the fa'amatai chiefly system.
tangentialFactors:
The territory's population is small, roughly 57,000 residents across seven islands and atolls, and hotel capacity skews toward business travel in Pago Pago. Social conservatism runs alongside cultural acceptance: Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved public behavior is expected regardless of orientation.

A 2003 legislative hearing recorded contemporaneous fa'afafine testimony that Samoan fa'afafine do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing, a view that complicates any assumption that local cultural acceptance maps onto advocacy for formal relationship recognition.
localsOnly:
Residents interact with a territorial government that has been sued successfully over treatment of transgender employees, with the US Justice Department securing a settlement in September 2023 and a federal civil action in June 2023 citing a hostile work environment for a transgender woman employed by the territorial government.

The Fono Senate's March 2003 rejection of a same-sex marriage ban bill, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it, remains the legislature's recorded position on the question; the local statutory ban nonetheless continues to be treated as operative in on-island legal analysis.

SOFIAS, formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, serves as the principal fa'afafine community organisation and frames its identity explicitly as cultural pride.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling is operative in American Samoa remains formally unresolved: territory officials have publicly questioned applicability, a 2026 law review article argues it applies and that a certificate must be issued on application, and no same-sex couple has yet applied for a license to test the question. The litigation roadmap through the High Court of American Samoa and the US Department of the Interior has not been initiated.

The constitutional durability of the local same-sex marriage ban under the 14th Amendment is an open research question, per a July 2024 survey, and no court has ruled on it.

The outcome of the ACLU's challenge to the federal passport policy in the courts is not sourced here, and the current practical posture for trans travelers renewing documents at US consulates abroad is not documented in this inventory.
